78.en: , the local populace is generally unaware of the Inquisition’s presence and has little reason to look for it. Though isolated individuals may suspect Inquisitorial activity, such sentiments are relatively rare and have little popular support or corroborating evidence, usually dismissed as the base-level paranoia common to Imperial society. The party’s disguises are mostly taken at face value, and if someone sees through them, the party are assumed to be charlatans, not Inquisitorial agents. Acts of infiltration or sabotage are generally attributed to local criminals, political rivals, cultists, or other more common scapegoats than the Inquisition. Strange things happen throughout the Imperium daily, but such is life amid the grim darkness of the 41st Millennium; there’s no reason the public should think anything more of it while Subtlety is Covert.

82.en: Maintaining Covert Subtlety typically requires the party to operate in the shadows, carefully leaving few traces of their clandestine activities. Alternatively, it could mean the party hides in plain sight while discouraging witnesses and investigators with leverage, misdirection, or outright fabrications. A Covert party’s presence and identity are unknown to the public, or their affiliation is obfuscated well enough to allow them to operate in the open while shifting blame and suspicion away from the Inquisition.

86.en: Under Covert conditions, the populace behaves normally. To some extent everyone in the Imperium is afraid all the time; of war, xenos, mutants, not being seen as working hard or faithful enough, afraid of being drafted for a tithe, or being stolen away by the Inquisition. Fear perpetuates, but in this scale of Subtlety, there is no suspicion or scrutiny towards the party. Mechanically, this means people are willing to give the party the benefit of the doubt when it seems they are up to something dubious. They must play on the public’s ambivalence, though actively, and leaning on that too hard or too often can eventually lead to suspicion. People are only willing to believe in so many coincidences before they develop real doubts.

182.en: , whispers of the Inquisition’s presence circulate, though incontrovertible proof remains sporadic or elusive. Seeds of paranoia sprout as the streets and the halls of power echo with questionable accounts and rumours. Common folk dare not tarry in public, unsettled by the notion of encountering hypothetical Inquisitors lurking in the shadows. Ambitious elites seek to expose heretical behaviour amidst their peers to curry favour for themselves. Cautious nobles examine their activities, expunging evidence of sin just in case sceptical eyes turn their way. Criminal organisations and heretical cults scour their membership for infiltrators, subjecting the unproven to brutal loyalty tests. Because the population is paying attention, suspicious activities the party commits will likely raise concerns about their true motives and allegiances.

186.en: Maintaining Suspicious Subtlety typically requires the party to maintain a semblance of plausible deniability about their affiliation, though their actions needn’t be entirely clandestine. Remaining Suspicious means the Inquisition’s involvement in the area is suspected yet remains unconfirmed. Alternatively, certain individuals may have discovered the party’s intent or patronage, but those individuals have yet to convince the general population.

194.en: Under Suspicious conditions, people tend to be on edge, looking over their shoulders in case someone is watching. Newcomers, strangers, and other unknowns are met with distrust, while familiar faces behaving oddly elicit wariness or open hostility. Even a normally-trustworthy acquaintance asking too many questions or making unusual requests is worthy of scrutiny; it wouldn’t be the first time someone sold out a friend to save their own skin. Mechanically, this unease and distrust mean the party has a harder time avoiding notice, concealing their identity, or obfuscating the motives behind their actions. However, they may be able to wield the Inquisition’s reputation more effectively.

286.en: , no doubt remains about the party’s intentions: their status as Inquisitorial agents is public knowledge. With the Inquisition’s presence confirmed, public paranoia reaches a fever pitch as panic and self-preservation run rampant. Citizens tremble in fear of arbitrary punishment, hiding from sight and anxiously trying to prove innocence when accosted. The truly desperate may volunteer or fabricate incriminating information about friends and loved ones to save themselves from His judgement. Religious leaders attract flocks of distressed zealots suddenly eager to prove their piety. Civic unrest disrupts local industry and commerce while Administratum officials are loath to answer for those shortfalls and lean on manufactorum taskmasters to drive their serfs with increased brutality. Heretic cults swell as the lost and damned seek refuge from scrutiny. Some go to ground to avoid investigation, but others prepare for violent confrontation.

Subtlety can’t increase again until after the current mission ends and the Inquisition, including the party, vacate the area (or at least appear to) for at least a week. After this time, the GM redetermines Subtlety if it becomes relevant later.

Their patron’s influence will go the extra mile with these organisations. On the other hand, their enemies will grow more desperate than they ever have been. 474.en: Last, the party should be aware of the fear their presence now garners, especially in the hearts of their supposed allies. Many will show their true colours in weakness or misplaced fervour. Others might supply the party with tools unfit for the job, more fearful of giving the Inquisition nothing to work with. Now more than ever, the party must be vigilant with everyone they deal with.
